raw_evidence.content: The Stanford-to-Valley pipeline was not an accident; it was deliberately engineered by one man. Frederick Terman, Stanford's dean of engineering (1944-1958) and later provost (1955-1965), is widely called the 'father of Silicon Valley.' Before WWII he worried that Stanford's best engineering graduates had to leave the West Coast to find work, so he set out to build an industry around the university. In 1951 he spearheaded the creation of Stanford Industrial Park (now Stanford Research Park), the first university-owned industrial park in the world, leasing Stanford land to high-tech firms he called Stanford's 'secret weapon.' Varian Associates signed the first lease, followed by Terman's own former students Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard. The flywheel of alumni founding companies next door to their alma mater started with Terman's design.

raw_evidence.label: Frederick Terman engineered the pipeline
raw_evidence.content: The Stanford-to-Valley pipeline was not an accident; it was deliberately engineered by one man. Frederick Terman, Stanford's dean of engineering (1944-1958) and later provost (1955-1965), is widely called the 'father of Silicon Valley.' Before WWII he worried that Stanford's best engineering graduates had to leave the West Coast to find work, so he set out to build an industry around the university. In 1951 he spearheaded the creation of Stanford Industrial Park (now Stanford Research Park), the first university-owned industrial park in the world, leasing Stanford land to high-tech firms he called Stanford's 'secret weapon.' Varian Associates signed the first lease, followed by Terman's own former students Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard. The flywheel of alumni founding companies next door to their alma mater started with Terman's design.

raw_evidence.label: The HP garage and the founding myth (1939)
raw_evidence.content: The dataset's oldest tech company, Hewlett-Packard, anchors the most famous origin story in business: the garage at 367 Addison Avenue in Palo Alto where Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard — both Terman's Stanford students — founded HP in 1939, building electronic test equipment on $538 of capital. California named the garage 'the birthplace of Silicon Valley' and made it a Historical Landmark in 1989; HP bought the house for $1.7 million in 2000 to preserve it. The garage is now a near-religious symbol of the lone-founder myth. But the myth obscures the real engine: HP existed because Terman steered his students toward staying, and the garage was the first node of a deliberately built network, not a bolt of lightning. The dataset shows the same year, 1939, as the start of the lineage.

raw_evidence.label: Frederick Terman engineered the pipeline
raw_evidence.content: The Stanford-to-Valley pipeline was not an accident; it was deliberately engineered by one man. Frederick Terman, Stanford's dean of engineering (1944-1958) and later provost (1955-1965), is widely called the 'father of Silicon Valley.' Before WWII he worried that Stanford's best engineering graduates had to leave the West Coast to find work, so he set out to build an industry around the university. In 1951 he spearheaded the creation of Stanford Industrial Park (now Stanford Research Park), the first university-owned industrial park in the world, leasing Stanford land to high-tech firms he called Stanford's 'secret weapon.' Varian Associates signed the first lease, followed by Terman's own former students Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard. The flywheel of alumni founding companies next door to their alma mater started with Terman's design.

raw_evidence.label: Caveats baked into the Wikidata method
raw_evidence.content: Three honesty caveats follow directly from how the data was built, and they must stay visible. First, the tech flag undercounts: 323 of 545 links have no industry recorded on Wikidata at all, so the 104 'tech' rows are a floor, not a census. Second, 'founded by' is broad — it captures not just companies but foundations, PACs, schools and research institutes; Elon Musk's 15 'foundings' include America PAC, the America Party and a school, so a raw founder ranking mixes ventures with civic and personal projects. Third, 'educated at Stanford' (P69) is loose: it does not distinguish a PhD from a brief enrollment, and Musk is famously listed even though he left a Stanford PhD program almost immediately. Finally, because co-founders each get their own row, a company like Sun Microsystems appears multiple times; you must de-duplicate on company_id for a true unique-company count.
